19938-recreations-of-christopher-north-v:
Christopher North was the pen name of John Wilson, Edinburgh professor and magazinist. His Recreations gather tales, essays, and sporting sketches. Volume two holds a child singing at a holy hour. She was as full of life as the star above her was of lustre. The hour tamed them both, the narrator says. At the party's bidding she renewed the strain. Wilson's lyric sentiment runs at full tide here.

Wilson co-created Blackwood's famous Noctes Ambrosianae dialogues. The Recreations collect his gentler, rural side. Angling, cottages, and Scottish scenery fill their pages. His prose influenced a generation of magazine writers. Volume two shows the sentiment Scots readers loved. Modern taste finds it lush; the craft is undeniable.
19973-the-mabinogion-vol-2:
Volume two of The Mabinogion continues Lady Charlotte Guest's Welsh tales. A great king's court assembles here in full splendor. Nine crowned kings, his tributaries, attend his high festivals. Earls and barons join them as invited guests. Such feasts mark Arthur's court in the Welsh telling. His dominion runs both by sea and by land. The Welsh Arthur is an emperor, not merely a king.

Guest's translation carried these tales to world readers in the 1840s. Volume two holds branches of the Mabinogi and native romances. Giants, hounds, and otherworld journeys crowd its pages. The prose keeps a bardic, formula-rich music. These stories are the deep source of much modern fantasy. Reading them is visiting the wellhead.
20109-reminiscences-of-sixty-years-in-pu:
George S. Boutwell published volume two of his Reminiscences of Sixty Years in Public Affairs in 1902. Boutwell served in Congress and in Grant's cabinet during stormy years. He recalls the Thirty-seventh Congress and its failed plans for compromise. Those fights split both parties before and during the Civil War.

One rival drew Democratic support as the People's Party candidate. Boutwell's own radical stand cost him backing from cautious Republicans. Such inside detail is the value of a long public memoir. Readers get war-era politics told by a man who voted, spoke, and served through it.
20539-letters-of-edward-fitzgerald-in-tw:
The second volume of Edward FitzGerald's letters carries his correspondence into his later years. The talk turns often to his famous translation of Omar Khayyam. Friends sent him copies, versions, and questions about the Persian poet he had made an English classic.

FitzGerald asks after a lithograph copy of Omar that a friend mentioned. My translation has its merit, he writes, but it misses a main one in Omar, which he will leave the friend to find out. He jokes in the same breath about Latin versions needing correction. The letters show his modesty, humor, and endless tinkering.
20646-the-nabob-vol-1-of-2:
The Nabob is the English version of Alphonse Daudet's great French novel Le Nabab, issued here in two volumes in 1898. It tells of a Tunisian adventurer who arrives in Paris with a fortune and buys his way toward power. This first volume opens with high praise for its author.

Henry James declared that Daudet stood at the head of his profession, and called him an admirable genius. Robert Louis Stevenson thought the same of Daudet's gift. The introduction gathers such verdicts before the story starts. Daudet's Paris of money, newspapers, and bought honors then unfolds in his bright, ironic style.
20778-sylva-or-a-discourse-of-forest-tre:
John Evelyn stands high among prose writers of the late seventeenth century, this edition notes. His Sylva, a discourse of forest trees, first came out in 1664. Volume one opens a work born of worry for England's shrinking woods.

Evelyn urges landowners to plant oaks and other trees for future fleets and homes. He mixes lore, craft, and sound growing advice for each kind. Sylva counts as an early call to care for forests as a public good. Gardeners and woodland lovers still read Evelyn for his zest and his deep store of tree craft.
20827-traditions-of-the-north-american-i:
Between two stormy seas lives young Chappewee in volume two of Traditions of the North American Indians. His father, the first of men, found a world rich in food and pleasant things. That first landing lay near the Dog-rib people's hunting grounds.

Creation tales and hero stories fill this second set of camp-fire traditions. James Athearn Jones took them from native tellers and early sources alike. Each tale shows how a people explained the world's start and shape. Read with care for its age, the volume keeps lore that oral memory alone once carried across long centuries of change.
20835-the-monctons-a-novel-volume-1-of-2:
Geoffrey Moncton, youngest son of a rich Yorkshire baronet, tells his family's tale. His father's hopes all centered on the first-born son, as custom ruled. Junior sons counted for little, yet Geoffrey still needed a gentleman's start in life.

An army commission, bought by Sir Robert, launches the young man's path. Volume one of The Monctons builds a world of rank, money, and family pride. The novel probes what younger sons did when birth order shut most doors. Its calm, period voice suits readers who like old family sagas told from inside the great house.
20934-the-natural-history-of-selborne-vo:
A full spring called the Well Head gave Selborne its name and its start, says volume two. Constant water drew the village to its side across the ages. Its rivulet grows, by Oakhanger, into a fair stream of the parish.

Gilbert White's second volume adds letters on fossils, weather, and rural lore. His Hampshire parish stays the whole stage, yet the world feels vast there. White notes swallows, tortoises, echoes, and old customs with one keen eye. Read with volume one, it completes a classic of close looking that made one small place stand for all nature.
21260-canada-and-the-canadians-vol-2:
Sir Richard Henry Bonnycastle, a lieutenant-colonel of Royal Engineers in Canada West, published this two-volume account of Canada in 1849. Volume Two returns to Toronto after a flight to Lake Superior, then travels to Hamilton by fast steamer. Loons, diving bells, and birds caught with hooks at Niagara fill the road.

Bonnycastle meets Peter Jones, the Ojibwe chief and missionary, and weighs the Family Compact, church quarrels, and the new university. He argues for the value of Canada's union with Britain against repeal talk. Public works spending and President Polk's Oregon claims also catch his engineer's eye. The book mixes travel, politics, and natural history.
21329-the-nabob-vol-2-of-2:
Alphonse Daudet's novel of Parisian money and manners closes in this second volume, translated by George Burnham Ives with an introduction by Brander Matthews. Chapters resume at A Day of Spleen and move through an exhibition, a public man, and the affair of the Jenkins pearls. The nabob of the title is a rich outsider buying his way into Paris society.

A clerk's memoirs appear twice, framing the great man's rise and ruin from inside his household. The first night of a play called Revolte, scenes at Bordighera, and the obsequies fill the closing movements. Daudet drew the tale from real Paris scandals of wealth, politics, and newspapers in the early Third Republic.
21513-the-life-and-adventures-of-peter-w:
Robert Paltock's Life and Adventures of Peter Wilkins first appeared in 1751, and volume one is given here. A. H. Bullen's preface, from the 1884 edition, praises the tale as a fine voyage of the imagination. Bullen laments how little is known of Paltock himself.

Wilkins is cast away and finds a strange land reached by flight, in the manner of a dream voyage. Winged folk and a new world test the hero's wits and heart. The tale stands near Robinson Crusoe and Gulliver in kind, yet has a charm all its own. Hazlitt and fame open Bullen's essay on why writers seek lasting names.
21665-a-brief-history-of-the-english-lan:
J. M. D. Meiklejohn compresses English studies in volume two of his Brief History of the English Language and Literature. The set covers grammar, word history, and the history of letters. Each part alone, the notice says, makes a good one year's course.

This part suits high schools and colleges, where the first suits high schools alone. Meiklejohn aims at the utmost clearness and simplicity throughout. He sets syntax out as firm rules, so young learners have solid ground. Pupil-teachers in England used the book through four years of study and a first college year, with verse grammar held for the fifth.
21851-history-of-the-negro-race-in-ameri:
Black Americans from 1800 to 1880 fill this second volume of George W. Williams's History of the Negro Race in America, published in 1883. Williams was the first Black member of the Ohio legislature and a judge advocate of the Grand Army of the Republic. His note says slavery grew with the Republic's growth until the sword parted them. He promises honest, impartial inquiry into the whole struggle over slavery's spread.

Six parts and twenty-nine chapters cover Black people as slaves, as soldiers, and as citizens. The wider work opens with the unity of mankind, a sketch of Africa, and the Black governments of Sierra Leone and Liberia. It was a landmark: a full history of Black America by a Black historian, built on records.
22021-gallipoli-diary-volume-2:
General Sir Ian Hamilton commanded the Allied force sent against Turkey at Gallipoli in 1915. His Gallipoli Diary, published in 1920, prints the journal he kept during the campaign. Volume II covers the last, hardest months. It begins with Lord Kitchener's advice and a visit from the Prime Minister's envoy.

Hamilton describes the August attacks at Sari Bair and Suvla, and how the Suvla landing collapsed. He argues with London, weighs the French plan, and watches the case for evacuation grow. Artillery reports fill the appendices. The diary is both a record and a defence, written by the man who carried the blame for a failed campaign.
22022-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-2:
Louisa May Alcott, the author of Little Women, issued Shawl-Straps as the second series of Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag. Alcott jokes in her opening pages that travel books are a fate no writer escapes. She had sworn never to write one, yet here it is. The book grew out of her tour of Europe in 1870 and 1871.

Alcott travelled with a younger companion through Brittany, Switzerland, Italy, and London. She writes about inns, peasants, pictures, and the small disasters of the road. Her tone is brisk, funny, and unsentimental. American readers at home got Europe through the eyes of "Aunt Jo," and the scrap-bag format let her mix sketches, stories, and chat.
22421-the-hesperides-noble-numbers-vol-1:
The Hesperides and Noble Numbers collect the poems of Robert Herrick in two volumes. An introduction notes a singular fact of English poetry. The first great age of lyric poetry matched the great age of drama.

The lyric school advanced steadily as the dramatic school declined. It declined from the bright promise of its dawn. Herrick stands near the center of that lyric flowering. His Hesperides holds secular songs of love, flowers, and country life. Noble Numbers adds his sacred poems to the set. Readers get a Cavalier poet's full range in one place. Short, musical lyrics make the volumes easy to dip into anywhere.
22567-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
E. Benjamin Andrews wrote a multi-volume History of the United States. Volume two's contents show the young nation forged by war. Military experience gained stands among its listed lessons and themes.

Nothing but war, Andrews argues, could have done this work. The population then was scattered across a vast country thinly. Difficulties of communication made unity harder still for the colonies. Other centrifugal influences pulled the states apart from one another. France was no longer a menace to the colonies after independence. Instead she became a natural friend and ally of America. Such themes carry the narrative through the Confederation and Constitution. Readers get scholarly nineteenth-century history with its arguments laid out plainly.
22689-the-confessions-of-a-caricaturist-:
The Confessions of a Caricaturist, volume 2, is the second half of Harry Furniss's memoir of life as a leading comic artist of Victorian London. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Furniss drew for Punch and illustrated books by Dickens and Carroll, and his confessions are stuffed with the famous faces he sketched.

The sample recalls a man who in 1887 startled the town with an artistic joke: a bold, full-scale parody of a Royal Academy exhibition, years in the making. Anecdotes of artists, actors, and politicians crowd the volume in that spirit. Furniss writes as an insider who loved the bohemian art world even while laughing at it. His memoir remains a rich source on the making of celebrity images.
22797-diderot-and-the-encyclop-dists-vol:
John Morley wrote Diderot and the Encyclopaedists, whose second volume completes his study of Denis Diderot and the men who made the great French Encyclopaedia. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Morley, a leading Victorian man of letters, treated the philosophes as heroes of free thought.

The sample turns to Diderot's own writings. It praises a dialogue Diderot published in 1773, the Conversation of a Father with His Children. The dialogue shows his taste for putting moral questions in an interesting way. The little dialogue, perfect in its simple, realistic form, asks a sharp question. May a man set his own judgment of special circumstances above the law of the land? Morley's second volume weighs such works one by one. The book remains a lucid English road into Enlightenment France.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-2: Volume two of the old ballads — Scottish chiefs, English bowmen, and star-crossed lovers — carries on Nichols' lively anthology. The past sings again in his spirited and faithful versions. A treasure for all ballad lovers. The old north country lives in every stanza.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co: Hank saves himself with an eclipse and becomes the Boss in this second part. His first miracles of Yankee ingenuity dazzle the court. Twain's comedy of anachronism hits its stride. An eclipse, a bonfire, and a fountain restore his prestige in fine style.
a-far-country-volume-2: The second volume deepens the hero's ambitious climb in A Far Country. Great success brings wealth but slowly hollows out the soul. The searching novel probes the true price of ambition. The tense middle passage of a sweeping tale.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-2: Howells's Hazard of New Fortunes, volume two: the early middle. The Marches settle in New York. The great novel builds. Realism's masterpiece, howells's novel builds, the Marches settle, realism grows, Howells, the middle, New York.
a-history-of-science-volume-2: Henry Smith Williams's second volume of popular science history, covering Rome, the Arabs, and the Middle Ages. Clear and engaging, it keeps the story of knowledge moving for general readers. The middle ages of science, vividly told.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-2: The second volume of A Woodland Queen follows the heroine's trials. Country loves and country sorrows shape her tender youth. The deep forest remains her sure and secret refuge. Theuriet's tender pastoral tale continues apace.
abigail-adams-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Abigail Adams's letters covers the presidency years and the early republic. John Adams was now in high office, and Abigail wrote from the center of the new nation's politics. The 1840 edition completes the set.

The letters treat the move to Washington, party fights, and the bitter Adams-Jefferson feud. Abigail judges public men with a dry wit and strong opinions of her own. Home and state business mix on every page, as they did in her life. Together the two volumes form America's most famous political correspondence between husband and wife. She also records the death of friends and the strain of public life.
amundsen-south-pole-vol-2:
The second volume of Roald Amundsen's The South Pole, in A. G. Chater's 1912 English translation, tells the dash itself. Five men with dogs set out from the Bay of Whales in October 1911. They reached the Pole on December 14, ahead of Scott's party.

Amundsen describes the climb onto the polar plateau, the careful marking of the pole site, and the fast run back. The party reached base in January with men and dogs in good shape. The volume also carries the voyage home and the scientific results. It is the winner's own telling of the race.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Volume two of Breasted's Ancient Records of Egypt, published in 1906, is devoted to the eighteenth dynasty. That dynasty built Egypt's empire: Thutmose III's campaigns in Syria, Hatshepsut's famous expedition to Punt, and the wealth of Amenhotep III fill its inscriptions. Breasted translates the annals, hymns, and tomb records reign by reign.

The volume catches Egypt at its height, when its armies reached the Euphrates and its temples rose at Thebes. Court biographies and victory stelae give the human grain inside the royal boasts. Breasted's corpus made such texts usable by every historian of the ancient world. Volume two is often the most read of the five. Its records anchor the chronology of the whole region.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-2:
Volume two of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson in 1885, gathers the Fathers of the second century. The writers here are Hermas, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, and Clement of Alexandria. The set as a whole is the standard English home of the early church writers.

Hermas's Shepherd, a book of visions on repentance, opens the volume. Tatian and Athenagoras defend the faith against pagan charges, while Theophilus writes to a pagan friend. Clement of Alexandria closes it, wedding Greek learning to Christian teaching. The volume shows the young church arguing for its life in a hostile empire.
appian-roman-history-white-vol-2:
The second volume of Appian's Roman History, in Horace White's 1899 English version, turns from foreign wars to the wars Rome fought on itself. Appian wrote in Greek around 160 CE. His five books on the civil wars run from the Gracchi brothers to Sextus Pompeius, the last holdout after the death of Caesar.

Here are the land reforms that split the city, the march of Sulla, the rise of Pompey and Caesar, and the death lists that killed Cicero. Appian tells it as one long fall from republic to one-man rule. His is the only connected ancient account of these wars, and still the fullest source for the end of the republic.
arabian-nights-lane-1848-vol-2:
Edward William Lane made the Nights scholarly in his Thousand and One Nights, and Volume II here is the 1848 printing. Lane's version, first published from 1838 to 1840, filled the tales with notes on Egyptian life and custom. Volume II completes the library's Lane set alongside its mates.

Lane trimmed what Victorian families could not read, yet his learning gave the tales new weight. His notes turn stories into a window on Cairo's streets, homes, and beliefs. Readers who want the Nights with a guide beside them still choose Lane, and this volume carries his middle nights.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-2:
Payne's second volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night, from 1882, keeps Shahrazad's nights unrolling. Tales of merchants, demons, and enchanted cities fill the Calcutta text that John Payne followed for his first complete English version. The frame holds: each dawn leaves a story hanging, and the king spares the teller one more day.

Victorian readers met in these pages a world of jinn and treasure that bowdlerized editions had hidden. Payne's plain, rich English let the Arabic storyteller's art speak without trimming. Volume II deepens the set's claim to completeness, night after marvelous night.
aristophanes-eleven-comedies-vol-2:
Volume two completes the eleven surviving comedies of Aristophanes, the master of Athenian Old Comedy. An anonymous English translation carries the set. The plays span the later years of his long career.

The Birds builds a city in the sky to escape Athenian folly. In Lysistrata, women end a war by withholding sex from their husbands. The Frogs stages a contest between dead tragedians in the underworld. Thesmophoriazusae, Ecclesiazusae, and Plutus round out the volume. Together they show comedy testing every Athenian institution, from the assembly to the gods. His last plays show comedy itself changing toward gentler, more domestic plots.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
Rogers's second Loeb volume of Aristophanes, published in 1924, holds The Peace, The Birds, and The Frogs. In The Peace a farmer flies to heaven on a dung beetle to rescue the goddess Peace from a pit. The Birds builds a city in the sky and starves the gods into terms.

The Frogs sends Dionysus to the underworld to fetch back a dead tragedian. There Aeschylus and Euripides contest in verse, weighed line by line like goods. Rogers renders the songs and slang in brisk rhyming verse. These three are among the most inventive comedies ever staged. The volume shows Aristophanes moving from topical satire toward pure fantasy.
arnold-history-rome-vol-2:
Rome strides toward world power in the second volume of Thomas Arnold's History of Rome, from 1843. The middle Republic fights the Punic Wars against Carthage. Victory at sea and in Spain and Africa makes Rome master of the western seas.

Arnold pairs firm learning with the moral eye of a great teacher. He asks what conquest did to the conquerors as well as the conquered. Generals and senates alike face his even judgment. The narrative carries readers from a city-state to an empire in the making, in prose that kept the work a Victorian classic for decades.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-2:
Volume two of Yonge's Deipnosophists continues Athenaeus's banquet of the learned. The guests keep eating, drinking, and quoting lost books at length. Courses of fish, fowl, and wine structure the endless conversation.

Cooks, flute-girls, philosophers, and parasites all receive learned discussion. Athenaeus piles quotation upon quotation from authors otherwise vanished. Parasites and flatterers get a famous taxonomy of their types. The talk ranges from Homer to the price of fish in Athens. Yonge's English carries the feast's second helping steadily. Readers taste how much ancient learning survived only inside other men's dinner talk here.
ausonius-evelynwhite-loeb-vol-2:
The second Loeb volume of Ausonius, in Hugh G. Evelyn White's translation, completes the poems of the Bordeaux master. Ausonius wrote in the late fourth century, when Gaul was rich, Christian in name, and still steeped in the old classics. His letters and later poems fill this volume.

Verse letters to his friend Paulinus press the monk-poet to leave his Spanish retreat, a plea Paulinus famously refused. Riddles, epigrams, and a strange cento stitched from Virgil show the playful side of his craft. Read with the first volume, the set gives the full Ausonius. Few poets show so well how the Roman world turned toward the medieval one.
autobiography-of-andrew-dickson-white-vo: Volume two of Andrew Dickson White's autobiography: the Cornell founder's later years, diplomacy, and the warfare of science. Distinguished, candid, and full of famous names. A great American life, continued. White's battles for science against dogma were heroic.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-2:
Volume two of Zwingli's Latin Works and Correspondence spans 1522 to 1528, the years when Zurich's reform took hold. William John Hinke edited the volume, published at Philadelphia in 1922 under the American Society of Church History. Translators Henry Preble, Walter Lichtenstein, and Lawrence A McLouth carried the Latin into English.

These are the years of open break: images removed, the mass set aside, and Zurich set on a new course. Zwingli's letters show him guiding a city through change while arguing with foes on every side. His treatises state the Swiss case in his own sharp terms. The volume forms the core of the English Zwingli set.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-2:
Volume two of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud finishes Tract Sabbath, begun in volume one. The 1918 edition carries the second half of the Sabbath discussions. Sabbath law was a daily test of faithfulness for observant Jews, and the rabbis treat it with care.

The talks turn to cooking, travel limits, and what may be moved or worn on the holy day. Case after case sharpens the line between rest and work. Rodkinson's plain English keeps the debates readable without flattening their logic. With volume one, it gives the full Sabbath tractate in English dress.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-2:
Akbar's reign rolls on in the second volume of Badauni's chronicle, in W. H. Lowe's 1899 English version. Court intrigue thickens, and debates on faith grow bolder at court. Badauni's private scorn for the emperor's bold experiments sharpens page by page.

He records grants, quarrels, hunts, and heresies in one blunt stream. The gap between the public glory and his secret doubts fascinates modern readers. Few Mughal sources read with such spice and attitude. Lowe's translation keeps the chronicler's bite, giving English readers a history that entertains even as it informs about power, faith, and pride.
bancroft-history-us-vol-2:
Colonial America deepens in the second volume of Bancroft's History of the United States, in the 1866 printing. New colonies rise, assemblies claim their rights, and self-rule takes root. A distinct American character begins to form across the seaboard.

Bancroft writes as the nation's celebrant, tracing one long march toward freedom. Town meetings, charters, and quarrels with royal governors all point forward. He finds destiny at work in small, stubborn acts of self-government. The volume builds the base of his democratic epic, the long colonial prelude without which the Revolution, in his view, cannot be understood.
bernal-diaz-vol-2:
Volume Two of Bernal Diaz's memoirs, in Lockhart's translation, brings the conquest of Mexico to its grim climax. Diaz, the old soldier, had set out to correct the grand histories with a ranker's memory. This volume holds his most harrowing chapters.

He describes the Spanish flight from Tenochtitlan on the Night of Sorrows and the long siege that followed. The city's fall, Cortes's later expeditions, and the conquerors' quarrels over spoils close the story. Diaz ends poor and unthanked in Guatemala, still proud of what the soldiers did. His eyewitness voice outlasted every official version of the conquest.
bibliotheca-chemica-a-catalogue-of-the-a: Bibliotheca chemica, 1906, second copy. The chemical library. This book preserves that catalogue. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. The historical record keeps it. Writers of history may cite it later.
blackstone-commentaries-sharswood-vol-2:
Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England appears here in Volume 2 of George Sharswood's edition, covering Books 3 and 4. Blackstone first published the Commentaries in the 1760s. Sharswood, an American judge, edited this 1893 form; the set's first volume, Books 1 and 2, is also live.

Book 3 treats private wrongs: how courts hear civil cases, juries work, and injuries are remedied. Book 4 treats public wrongs, the criminal law, from treason and murder to trial and punishment. Blackstone wrote English law as a clear, ordered whole that lay readers could grasp. The Commentaries taught generations of lawyers in Britain and America their first law.
brant-ship-of-fools-barclay-vol-2:
More fools board the ship in Volume Two of Barclay's English Ship of Fools, the 1874 Jamieson edition of Brant's satire. Flatterers, drunkards, and the learned-ignorant take their places among the crew. The remaining chapters of the 1494 original complete the voyage toward the land of fools.

Verse satire and woodcut portraits keep the moral medicine entertaining to the last page. Brant's targets, from corrupt clergy to vain scholars, rarely feel dated. Barclay's Tudor English adds a second layer of period charm for modern readers. Together the two volumes hold Renaissance Europe's most famous satire entire. The journey ends where it began, with human folly undefeated and oddly lovable.
bryce-american-commonwealth-vol-2:
State and local life fill the second volume of Bryce's American Commonwealth, from 1888. Bryce turns from Washington to governors, townships, parties, and the press. Public opinion, he argues, is the true sovereign of the republic.

He shows democracy at ground level, in caucuses, courts, and city halls. Parties appear as vast machines that both serve and strain the system. His eye for flaw and strength stays even throughout. The volume completes a classic study. It understood America from the bottom up as fully as from the top down, and it still rewards close reading today.
burton-pilgrimage-medinah-meccah-vol-2:
The second volume of Burton's Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to El-Medinah and Meccah completes his 1853 journey. Volume one reached Medina, the Prophet's city and burial place. Burton, still in disguise as a pilgrim, now presses on to Mecca itself. The Memorial edition text is used here.

He performs the rites of the Hajj among the crowds: circling the Kaaba, drinking from the well of Zamzam, and standing on the plain of Arafat. His notes on the rites remain among the fullest ever made by an outside observer. The volume closes with the return journey and his appendices. The pilgrimage book made Burton the most famous traveler of his age.
byron-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Byron's Letters and Journals, edited by Prothero in 1898, covers the years of marriage, scandal, and exile. Byron wed Annabella Milbanke in 1815, and the marriage collapsed within a year amid dark rumors. In 1816 he left England forever.

The letters follow him to Switzerland, where he met Shelley and wrote through a haunted summer, then on to Venice. He is by turns bitter, funny, tender, and reckless. Prothero prints the record with care, letting Byron's own voice dominate. Few letter writers of any age match his energy on the page. His letters to his publisher Murray mix business, gossip, and bravado.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-2:
Civil War fills the second volume of Carlyle's Cromwell, in the 1904 Lomas edition. Letters from camp and council trace the revolution as it unfolds. Cromwell the soldier and statesman speaks in terse, godly, driven prose.

Battles, sieges, and hard choices crowd the years covered here. Carlyle's commentary blazes beside the texts he prints. Readers hear the war in the first person, from the man at its center. The volume gives history a rare texture. Orders, prayers, and reports were written in the press of events by a leader who felt God's hand in each turn.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-2:
War over the Austrian succession fills the second volume of Carlyle's life of Frederick the Great, from 1865. The young king gambles his new crown on bold marches and pitched battles. His triumph shocks the old courts of Europe.

Carlyle turns dry campaigns into epic poetry with sheer force of prose. He admires nerve, speed, and iron will above all virtues. Councils, camps, and freezing bivouacs pass in vivid rush. Readers feel war as the king's stern school, where Prussia's fate hung each season on one man's nerve and the loyalty of his hard-pressed troops.
cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-volume-: Fanny Burney's Cecilia continues as the young heiress navigates London's fashionable dangers — fortune-hunters, false friends, and the pride that threatens her happiness. This second volume deepens the comedy and the feeling. Burney at her sparkling best. Balls, beaux, and bad advisers test her judgment in chapters sparkling with Burney's wit.
chambers-cyclopaedia-1728-vol-2:
The second volume of Chambers's Cyclopaedia followed the first in 1728, completing the universal dictionary of arts and sciences. Chambers had set out to gather all useful knowledge between two covers, in plain alphabetical order. With this volume, the design stood whole.

Volume 2 carries the alphabet to Z, treating the later sciences, trades, and terms of art with the same cross-referenced method. Readers could enter at any word and follow the links through the whole circle of learning. cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-2:
Caesar's rise darkens the second volume of Cicero's letters, in Shuckburgh's 1899 version. The Republic slides toward its death throes year by year. Cicero endures exile, wins return, and watches old freedoms fail around him.

He writes to friends in hope one week and despair the next. Power gathers into fewer and fewer hands in his reports. The greatest letter writer of antiquity records his world's end in real time. Readers gain both fine drama and rich fact here, since no source shows the texture of late republican life, its fears and favors, half so well.
comte-positive-philosophy-martineau-1853:
Volume 2 of The Positive Philosophy of Auguste Comte appeared in Harriet Martineau's English version in 1853. Comte, the French founder of positivism, ranked the sciences and traced how human thought moves from theology to science. Martineau condensed his six French volumes into two clear English ones.

Volume 2 reaches the higher sciences and Comte's new science of society, which he helped name sociology. He argued that social life, like nature, follows laws that study can find. Martineau's version, praised by Comte himself, completed the English Positive Philosophy. Through it, British and American readers met positivism in a form they could actually finish, and debates on science and society changed.
critical-and-historical-essays-volume-2: Volume two of Macaulay's essays: Clive, Hastings, and the history of England in his unmatched prose. The reviews that taught a nation its past. Brilliant, confident, and endlessly readable. His Hastings essay is the greatest of all reviews.
curtius-history-greece-vol-2:
Tyrants and lawgivers rule the second volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. The archaic age sees Greek cities test one form of rule after another. From these trials the polis, the self-governing city-state, is born.

Solon, Sparta's stern order, and thriving colonies fill the account. Curtius traces how Greece hit on its most original gift to politics. Trade, verse, and law grow together in his broad picture. The volume shows a world of rival cities learning freedom the hard way, long before Athens rose to the height that later volumes celebrate in full.
darwin-descent-of-man-vol-2:
The second volume of Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man appeared with the first in 1871. Darwin gives most of it to his theory of sexual selection, first sketched in volume one. The volume closes his full case for the evolution of man.

Bird by bird and beast by beast, Darwin shows how mates choose by song, color, horns, and display. He argues such choices shaped the peacock's tail and much of human variety too. The book's closing chapters turn to mankind itself. Together, the two volumes caused a storm that has never fully settled.
darwin-life-and-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Darwin's Life and Letters, edited by his son Francis in 1887, covers fame and its costs. The Origin of Species appeared in 1859, and Darwin's quiet home at Down became the center of a scientific revolution. His letters carry the fight.

Friends like Huxley, Hooker, and Gray defend evolution in public while Darwin works at home. The Descent of Man and his books on plants and worms follow in turn. Ill health, family sorrow, and steady kindness mark the private record. The volume closes with his death and burial in Westminster Abbey in 1882. His working habits, down to his daily walks, come out in the letters.
davis-rise-and-fall-vol-2:
Volume Two of Davis's Rise and Fall, also from 1881, turns from argument to the war itself. Davis narrates the campaigns, his quarrels with generals, and the collapse of the Confederacy. He writes from the Confederate White House point of view.

He defends his choices on strategy, appointments, and the defense of Richmond. The fall of the capital, his flight, and his capture close the narrative. Davis shows little doubt and less regret, which shapes how historians use the book. Read beside the memoirs of Grant and Sherman, it completes the war's great triangle of command accounts.
demosthenes-public-orations-pickard-vol-:
Demosthenes was Athens' greatest public speaker in the fourth century BCE. Arthur Wallace Pickard-Cambridge translated his public orations, and volume two completes the set. On the Crown, his most famous speech, anchors the volume.

Demosthenes spent years warning Athens about Philip of Macedon's growing power. The Philippics urged resistance, while the Olynthiacs pleaded for aid to allies. On the Crown defends his whole career against a rival's prosecution. His sentences build like waves, mixing law, history, and patriotism. Pickard-Cambridge keeps the argumentative fire readable. Together with volume one, the set preserves Greek oratory at its peak.
dialogues-of-the-buddha-vol-2:
Volume two of the Dialogues of the Buddha, translated by T. W. and Caroline Rhys Davids in 1910, continues the Digha Nikaya's long discourses. The middle suttas of the collection stand here. The talks range over courts, groves, and debating halls of the Buddha's India.

The great discourse on the origin of things retells creation as a slow fall from light into craving and kingship. Other talks weigh sacrifice, self-mortification, and the bliss of meditation in careful steps. The Buddha often teaches by parable and by questions that turn the hearer around. The Rhys Davids version keeps the Pali's dignity in plain English.

dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-2:
Books twelve through thirty-five of the Roman History of Dio Cassius survive, like the first books, only in fragments. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation carries them in this second volume. Dio wrote around 230 CE, and Byzantine excerptors saved these pieces after the full text of the early books was lost.

The fragments track the takeover of the Mediterranean world by Rome. They cover the defeat of Macedon, the ruin of Carthage and Corinth, and wars in Spain and the east. The full history ran to eighty books and is the broadest Roman narrative that survives. This volume bridges the lost early books and the whole books that follow.
diodorus-library-booth-vol-2:
Volume Two of Booth's Diodorus holds Books Eleven through Twenty of the Library of History. The Sicilian's survey now reaches firmer historical ground. Greek wars and the rise of Macedon fill these books.

Persian invasions, the Peloponnesian War, and Alexander pass in review. Later books cover the heirs who split Alexander's empire. Diodorus often copies good sources that else are lost. That habit makes him vital despite a plain style. The volume is a big, useful store of ancient history, much of it found nowhere else in full. Scale and survival give the set its worth.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
Books three through five of the Roman Antiquities of Dionysius of Halicarnassus appear in this second volume of Edward Spelman's 1758 English version. Dionysius wrote around 7 BCE. His tale now moves from the later kings to the birth of the republic.

Tullus Hostilius and the Tarquins rule, fall, and give way to consuls. The young republic fights its neighbors and strains between rich and poor at home. Dionysius tells these years at great length, with speeches he composed for the actors. His account is the fullest that survives for the last kings and the first decades of free Rome.

Primes, even and odd numbers, and perfect numbers receive proofs. Euclid shows that the primes never run out in Book Nine. The bedrock of arithmetic was set down twenty-three centuries ago here. Heath's commentary connects each proposition to later mathematics with care.

Orestes, half mad after the deed, faces trial by his own city. Iphigenia in Taurica turns a priestess of human sacrifice toward rescue and escape. Andromache shows Hector's widow crushed between a new mistress and old grief. Cyclops, the lone surviving satyr play, plays the Polyphemus tale for rough laughs. evliya-travels-hammer-vol-2:

Evliya is half Marco Polo and half gossip columnist in these pages. He loves a good story and rarely lets doubt spoil one. Yet his detail on daily Ottoman life is rich and rare. Readers who finish this volume will grasp why his Seyahatname, the book of travels, stands unmatched as a portrait of an empire at ease with itself.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-2:

Freeman narrates the most famous year in English history at unmatched length. Marches, omens, shield walls, and the fatal arrow all get their due. He writes as scholar and as Saxon partisan at once. No fuller telling of the two battles exists, and readers who want the Conquest in depth, day by day and source by source, start their study here.
freytag-soll-und-haben-bd-2:

Love, loyalty, and loss test the young merchant to his core. Freytag closes his epic of commerce with the triumph of steady character. The ledger's two heads, debit and credit, frame a whole ethic of life. In its own tongue, the book shows the style that taught a rising class to see itself as worthy of serious fiction.
froissart-chronicles-johnes-vol-2:

Revolts shake both kingdoms here: the peasants of England and the towns of Flanders rise and are crushed. The volume ends with Richard's fall to Henry Bolingbroke, told with an eye for ceremony and doom. Froissart's index closes the set. His chronicle remains the fullest narrative of the fourteenth century's wars and courts.
froude-english-ireland-vol-2:
Secret societies stalk the second volume of Froude's Irish history, from 1872. The Whiteboys swear oaths and strike by night in the countryside. The Volunteers arm in the towns, and government loses its grip year by year.

Froude traces the long slide toward the rising of 1798. Grievance piles on grievance as reform fails again and again. His vivid style carries readers through a century of trouble. All his strong opinions stand on display, for friend and foe to judge. The volume forms the tense middle of his Irish tale, where patience runs out and violence gathers its forces.

The account stirred fierce dispute among clergy and scholars alike. It remains a gripping, partisan telling of the birth of the English Reformation.

gellius-attic-nights-rolfe-loeb-vol-2:
Books six through thirteen of the Attic Nights of Aulus Gellius fill this second Loeb volume, in John C. Rolfe's translation. Gellius wrote in the second century, gathering notes from his reading in Rome and Athens. The middle books keep the same free, curious range as the first.

Questions of grammar sit beside court cases, ghost tales, old Roman rites, and lines from poets whose works are lost. Gellius loves a puzzle: why a word means what it does, or how an old law read. His quotes save fragments of early Latin plays and speeches found nowhere else. The volume is a storehouse for anyone who loves the byways of Roman life.
godwin-political-justice-1793-vol-2:
Volume two of Godwin's Political Justice, also from 1793, completes his enquiry. The first volume laid down the rule of private judgment against government. This volume turns to property, the root of much rule in his view. Great wealth, he argues, breeds dependence and warps both rich and poor.

He sketches a society held together by reason and voluntary fairness. Human perfectibility, the slow growth of minds toward truth, anchors his hope. The two volumes together complete the work as issued. Later anarchists drew deeply on Godwin's pages. His vision of a stateless order starts here. The style is cool where the claims are hot.
goethe-wilhelm-meister-carlyle-1824-vol-:
Volume 2 of Carlyle's Wilhelm Meister appeared in 1824, continuing Goethe's novel of Wilhelm's apprenticeship and travels. Thomas Carlyle's translation carried the second half of Wilhelm's theater years and beyond. Wilhelm moves among actors, estates, and a secret society that watches his growth.

Encounters with the strange Mignon and the Harper deepen the book's mix of song, sorrow, and mystery. Wilhelm's mistakes in love and art slowly teach him the limits of the stage life he craved. Goethe used the tale to ask how a person forms a self in a changing world. Carlyle's English made that question part of British literary debate.
govdocs-archive_org-kalevala-the-land-of:
The Kalevala is Finland's national epic, built by Elias Lönnrot from rune-songs he collected from singers in Finland and Karelia. Volume 2, in the Berserker Books edition, holds the second half of the poem, carrying the long story that volume 1 began to its close.

Here the heroes Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Lemminkäinen move through quests, weddings, feuds, and the forging and loss of the Sampo, the magic mill that brings wealth. The verse keeps the driving rhythm of the original sung runes, in English dress. For Finns the Kalevala is a founding book; this volume finishes it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CBSPart2_CBS_Pa: Harold Weisberg wrote to George Herman of CBS News on March 30, 1974, one of hundreds of letters the assassination author sent to the journalists who covered the case. Weisberg spent decades arguing that the press had failed on the Kennedy story, and he argued it directly, by mail, to the men and women on the air. The letter is filed with material on CBS's coverage of the assassination. It is kept as part of his media correspondence in the archive.
gregory-tours-history-franks-dalton-vol-:
Volume two of Dalton's 1927 translation completes Gregory of Tours' History of the Franks, the ten books of Merovingian history finished in 594. The later books are Gregory's own times, the richest and darkest of the set. He writes as bishop of Tours from 573, in the middle of the events.

Kings Chilperic and Guntram, and the queens Fredegund and Brunhild, drive a story of assassinations, civil wars, and church councils. Gregory records his own trials: accused before kings, sheltering fugitives in his church, and defying royal tax men. Saints' miracles thread through the politics. The volume ends with his survey of his own episcopate. It is the best single source on the Frankish kingdoms.
grihya-sutras-oldenberg-vol-2:
Hermann Oldenberg translated the second volume of the Grihya Sutras in 1892. It appeared as volume thirty of the Sacred Books of the East. The Grihya Sutras give rules for Vedic domestic ceremonies in the home.

Birth, naming, first feeding, and the child's first haircut receive rites. Marriage ceremonies and funeral customs occupy large sections of the texts. Grand public sacrifices fill other books, but these sutras show religion at the family hearth. Oldenberg was a leading German scholar of early Indian religion. His volume preserves the texture of ordinary ancient Indian life. Intimate antiquity, rather than royal splendor, defines these pages throughout.
haeckel-evolution-of-man-vol-2:
The second volume of Haeckel's Evolution of Man, from 1874, turns from the embryo to the family tree. Where volume one traced man's growth before birth, this one traces the descent of mankind itself. Haeckel, Darwin's German bulldog, writes with total confidence.

He builds the genealogical tree of the human race, linking man through the apes and lower mammals to the earliest vertebrates. He even names a missing ancestor, Pithecanthropus alalus, the speechless ape-man, decades before Dubois found Java Man and made the guess look prophetic. The volume completes his popular account of human origins, dated in detail but huge in influence.
haeckel-history-of-creation-vol-2:
Volume two of Haeckel's History of Creation completes his 1868 survey of evolution. Volume one laid down the general doctrine; this one works through the special morphology and family history of organisms. Man's place among the primates is its destination.

Haeckel classifies life form by form, drawing the famous genealogical trees that branch from simple monera to mankind. He assigns each group its ancestors and its age in Earth history. The certainty outruns the evidence, as critics noted even then. Even so, the book's trees taught two generations to picture descent. It remains the boldest family album of nineteenth-century Darwinism.
hafez-divan-clarke-1891-vol-2:
The second volume of H. Wilberforce Clarke's Divan of Hafez, from 1891, completes the first full English rendering of Persia's beloved poet. Hafez sang in Shiraz in the fourteenth century, and his lyrics are still quoted daily across the Persian world. Clarke's prose keeps his copious commentary running beside the poems.

More ghazals follow here, with the odes, fragments, and longer pieces that close the Divan in its set order. Wine and the beloved carry the double sense Clarke labors to unfold: earthly joy and the soul's thirst for God. His two volumes are a library in themselves. With this one, the English reader holds the whole Hafez of the Victorian scholars.
haft-paikar-wilson-1924-vol-2:
Volume II of Wilson's Haft Paikar, from 1924, holds the commentary that partners his translation. Notes unpack Nizami's allusions, names, customs, and verses line by line for the English reader. The companion assumes the translation in hand and works as its guide through a dense Persian classic.

Scholars use the commentary to trace sources and untangle the poem's rich wordplay. Without it, much of the Seven Beauties' art would pass unseen by a foreign reader. The two Wilson volumes together, text and notes, form the first complete English presentation of Nizami's romance, issued in Probsthain's Oriental Series.
hallam-constitutional-history-vol-2:
Civil war and republic fill the second volume of Hallam's Constitutional History, from 1827. Parliament defies the king, war follows, and Cromwell rules in the Interregnum. Hallam finds the roots of modern liberty amid the chaos of the sixteen forties.

He treats both royalists and parliament men with cool fairness. Charters, trials, and ordinances pass under his lawyer's eye in turn. His liberal passion burns beneath a surface of strict calm. The volume shows a constitution tested by the sword and remade by law, a key chapter in the long tale of how England learned self-rule.
hallam-middle-ages-vol-2:
Spain, the Eastern Empire, and the Crusades fill the second volume of Hallam's View of the Middle Ages, in the 1863 printing. His gaze moves beyond France and England to the whole medieval world. Kingdoms, caliphates, and crusading hosts interact across three continents in his account.

Hallam's method was bold for its day: Europe read as one system. He compares laws, faiths, and governments across wide borders. Constantinople and Cordoba stand beside Paris in his broad canvas. The volume shows a historian thinking in civilizations, long before that habit grew common, and it widens his survey into a true portrait of an age.
handy-andy-a-tale-of-irish-life-volume-2: Samuel Lover's Handy Andy continues his blundering, big-hearted way through Irish life in this second volume. The most famous Irish comic novel, full of bulls, blunders, and laughter. Lover at his rollicking best. His Irish bulls and blunders have kept readers laughing for generations.
hawkesworth-account-voyages-southern-hem:
Volume two of John Hawkesworth's Account of the Voyages, the official 1773 record of Britain's Pacific expeditions, turns from Cook to the captains before him. It holds the circumnavigations of Commodore Byron, Captain Wallis, and Captain Carteret in the 1760s. Hawkesworth shaped their journals into one narrative.

Byron's Dolphin, Wallis's voyage in the same ship, and Carteret's battered Swallow each circle the globe in turn. Wallis's landfall at Tahiti in 1767, the island's first European contact, is the volume's famous scene. The accounts mix hard seamanship with first meetings between peoples who had never heard of each other. Cook's greater voyages frame the set.
heath-history-greek-mathematics-vol-2:
Volume two of Heath's History of Greek Mathematics appeared in 1921 with the first. It carries the story from Aristarchus to Diophantus, the later flowering. Astronomy, conic sections, and algebra dominate these later centuries.

Archimedes receives the attention his genius demands in these chapters. Apollonius's conics and Hipparchus's astronomy show Greek science at full stretch. Ptolemy's system and Diophantus's algebra close the ancient story. Heath tells the tale with a translator's closeness to his sources. He had personally Englished most of the major texts he discusses. The golden age and its brilliant aftermath fill the volume. Together, Heath's two volumes remain unmatched as a single-author survey. It is clear, full, and fair to all sides.
herodotus-histories-macaulay-vol-2:
Volume Two of Macaulay's Herodotus holds Books Five through Nine of the Histories. The Greek writer brings his great subject to its climax here. Persia invades Greece with a vast host by land and sea.

Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea anchor the tale. Herodotus honors brave stands and questions easy glory alike. He records speeches, omens, and the views of both sides. The result is the base account of the Persian Wars. Every later telling leans on his pages, and his eye for human motive keeps them fresh. Macaulay's prose keeps the pace swift throughout.
hippocrates-genuine-works-adams-vol-2:
Volume two of Adams's Hippocrates turns to the surgeon's art in ancient Greece. Fractures, dislocations, and wounds receive the detailed treatment here. The Hippocratic writings in this volume date from around 400 BCE.

Doctors learn to set bones with traction, splints, and bandaging. The famous Hippocratic bench for reducing dislocations gets full description. Head wounds and their trepanning dangers occupy careful chapters. Method feels practical, exact, and startlingly modern in many passages. Adams's surgical experience made him an ideal translator for this material. Ancient doctors setting bones show a skill that impresses modern surgeons. Volume one holds the theory; this volume holds the hands.
histoire-de-la-philosophie-hermetique-ac: Histoire de la philosophie hermetique, 1742, second copy. The hermetic history. This book preserves that work. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
historia-augusta-magie-vol-2:
David Magie's second Loeb volume of the Historia Augusta, from 1924, plunges into the worst years of the third century. The lives here cover the two Maximini, the three Gordians, and the joint emperors Maximus and Balbinus. The work itself dates to about 400 CE and pretends to have six authors.

Short reigns follow one another: soldier emperors raised by armies and cut down in months. The tales mix real campaign reports with court gossip and invented papers. Even so, for these dark decades the Historia Augusta is often the only connected source. Magie's notes help readers sort the fact from the fun.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: Gibbon's second volume traces Rome's third-century crisis: soldier-emperors, plague, invasion, and near-collapse, then recovery under Diocletian. The drama of an empire almost dying and pulling itself back makes this one of the most exciting stretches of the great history. Gibbon's irony never flags, even as the body count rises.
hobhouse-morals-evolution-1906-vol-2:
Part two of Morals in Evolution, also from 1906, completes Hobhouse's comparative ethics. The first part traced moral ideas from primitive groups toward civilized society. This part treats the higher morality and its place in the modern state. Hobhouse asks what ethics becomes when reason tests custom directly.

He weighs the claims of duty, the good, and rational self direction. The modern state appears as both a moral agent and a moral problem. His survey closes with ethics as a guide for social reform. The two parts together complete the work as planned. Readers gain a full map of his moral evolution scheme. It stands as a major Edwardian synthesis.
hortulus-hermeticus-flosculis-philosopho: Hortulus hermeticus, 1627, second copy. The hermetic garden. This book preserves that alchemy. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The historical record keeps it. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
human-science-or-phrenology-its-principl: Human Science, or Phrenology, 1873, second copy. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-2:
Volume two of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's 1849 English translation, turns from nature itself to the human mind facing nature. Humboldt calls it the history of the contemplation of the physical world. Few science books have a second volume like it.

He traces how poetry, landscape painting, and gardens have carried the feeling for nature through the ages. Then he follows the growth of physical knowledge: Egyptians, Greeks, Arabs, the age of Columbus, and the telescope and microscope. The volume is a history of science and art in one. It shows Humboldt the humanist, as learned in verse and paint as in rocks and stars.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Volume two of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Helen Maria Williams's translation, continues the 1799 to 1804 expedition through Venezuela. Humboldt and Bonpland push inland from the coast toward the great plains and the Orinoco. The seven-volume English set began in 1814.

The travelers cross the llanos, the vast grass plains, in crushing heat, studying electric eels and the life of the rivers. Humboldt tests the eel's shock on himself and records it in cool detail. He gathers plants, fixes positions by the stars, and questions missionaries on the peoples of the interior. Science and adventure run in one stream, as always with Humboldt.
huxley-life-and-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Huxley's life and letters, edited by his son Leonard in 1900, covers the later career. Thomas Henry Huxley was now a public figure, shaping schools, museums, and debate. The letters run to his death in 1895.

Later battles over science teaching and religious doubt fill many pages. Huxley's work with the Metaphysical Society and his essays on faith appear here too. A full index closes the two-volume set. Together they record how one man helped make science a central voice in British public life. Family letters soften the public image of the fierce debater.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-2:
Vikings and rival kings fill the second volume of William Archer's 1908 English Ibsen. The Vikings at Helgeland and The Pretenders dramatize Norway's medieval past with saga-like force. Sea kings, proud women, and contested crowns drive both plays toward blood and fate.

Ibsen soaked himself in the Icelandic sagas and made their world speak on stage. The Pretenders, his longest historical drama, follows Haakon's rise against the brooding Earl Skule. Passion for Norway's past made Ibsen his country's national poet of the stage. These plays hold the raw material from which the later realist forged his art. English readers meet them in the translation that introduced Ibsen abroad.
idrisi-geographie-jaubert-vol-2:
Africa and Asia fill the second tome of Jaubert's 1836 French version of al-Idrisi's geography. The survey, made in 1154 for Roger of Sicily, moves through seas and islands to the far East. Muslim knowledge of the earth here reaches its medieval height.

Al-Idrisi records routes, ports, peoples, and wonders with a clerk's care. His world stretches from Atlantic isles to the coasts of China. Kings and scholars across faiths prized the work for centuries. The volume completes a monument of medieval learning, one that shows how wide the horizons of the twelfth century could be in learned hands.
ihne-history-rome-vol-2:
Italy falls to Rome sword by sword in the second volume of Ihne's History, from 1871. The Samnite wars test the young republic to its limits. Pyrrhus crosses from Greece with his elephants and wins battles, yet loses the war for Italy's mastery.

Ihne shows Rome's rise step by step, campaign by campaign. Alliances, colonies, and roads bind the peninsula into one system. The republic learns to absorb beaten foes as partners in power. His systematic narrative pleased a generation of serious readers. The volume forms the solid middle base of a history long taken as the standard Roman account in English.
irving-knickerbocker-history-1809-vol-2:
Washington Irving's second volume of Knickerbocker's History of New York, published with the first in 1809, carries the mock-chronicle through the colony's great days and its fall. Diedrich Knickerbocker, Irving's invented Dutch historian, grows more partisan as the English threat nears. His solemn voice makes the absurdities funnier.

The volume's glory is Peter Stuyvesant, the peg-legged governor who storms about defending New Amsterdam against Swedes, Yankees, and finally the English fleet. Battles, councils, and feasts fill the closing chapters, all treated with epic gravity and comic deflation. When the Dutch surrender, Knickerbocker's world ends with them. The two volumes together founded American comic literature and gave New York its founding mythology.
isbe-1915-vol-2:
The second volume of the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia appeared in 1915, edited by the Scottish theologian James Orr. The set was the great conservative Bible reference of its generation, built by scholars who held traditional faith and modern learning together. Volume 2 carries the work through the middle reaches of the alphabet.

History, biography, geography, and doctrine continue in full measure, with signed articles and the same high standard as the first volume. Entries draw on the archaeology and language study of the day to fill in the world behind the text. Pastors and students used the set as their trusted companion for sermon and study alike. Read today, the volume also shows what mainline scholarship of 1915 believed about the Bible's world, stated by its own leading voices.
james-bostonians-1886-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Bostonians, published in 1886, brings the struggle over Verena Tarrant to its climax. Olive Chancellor wants Verena for the feminist cause and for herself. Basil Ransom wants her for a wife, and for the quiet home he thinks women belong in.

Verena's fame as a speaker grows while her two claimants tighten their hold. A summer at Cape Cod, concerts, and a final great meeting in a Boston music hall raise the stakes. Ransom's courtship turns into a siege, and Verena's own wishes are the last thing anyone consults. The ending, often read as grim beneath its surface, closes one of James's most argued-about novels.
james-portrait-of-a-lady-1881-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Portrait of a Lady, published with the first in 1881, carries Isabel Archer into the marriage she chose so freely. The novel's first half gave her money, travel, and suitors. This half tests what her freedom was worth.

Isabel marries Gilbert Osmond, the refined expatriate collector, and slowly sees the trap: he values her as an object in his collection. His former lover, Madame Merle, helped arrange the match for her own reasons. A deathbed revelation and a final interview in Rome expose the whole design. Isabel's choice in the last pages, to return to Rome, remains one of fiction's most debated endings.
james-wings-of-the-dove-1902-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Wings of the Dove moves the story to Venice. There Milly Theale rents a palace for her last season. Kate Croy's design, built in the London chapters of the first volume, now closes around its victim. The reckoning James prepares is quiet and devastating.

Densher stays in Venice after Kate leaves, and his conscience turns against the plot he serves. Milly learns the truth from a rejected suitor and, in James's famous phrase, turns her face to the wall. Her death, and the letter she leaves behind, change the meaning of her fortune entirely. The novel ends with two people who can never go back. Milly's strange posthumous victory completes the design.
jataka-cowell-vol-2:
Volume two of Cowell's Jataka, issued in 1895 alongside the first, continues the tales of the Buddha's former births. Cowell edited the six-volume Cambridge set, with W. H. D. Rouse and others translating from the Pali. The numbering of the 547 tales runs on from volume one.

The Bodhisatta, the being who will become the Buddha, now lives as birds, beasts, ascetics, and kings. Each birth turns on a choice: greed punished, mercy rewarded, a promise kept at cost. Frame verses give the point, and the Buddha's closing words name who each figure became. The volume deepens the great story cycle of Buddhist Asia.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume-2:
Volume two of Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of John Lothrop Motley opens in 1860. Its sixteenth chapter finds Motley in England as the American Civil War breaks out. He had just published the first two volumes of his History of the Netherlands. The crisis at home pulled him back from past centuries to his own country's fight.

Motley wrote two long letters to the London Times explaining the Union cause to Europe. Holmes, backed by William Everett's testimony, calls their effect great and timely. In 1861 Motley returned to America and was appointed minister to Austria by Lincoln. Holmes draws on letters from Motley's daughter, Lady Harcourt, for the Vienna years that follow.
joseph-andrews-vol-2:
Volume two of Joseph Andrews continues Henry Fielding's comic novel within his collected works, edited by George Saintsbury. The contents pick up Book Two at chapter fourteen. Parson Adams meets Parson Trulliber, in an interview readers long remember. Adams's forgetfulness then lands him in a fresh adventure.

Book Three opens with praise of biography, then a night scene of wonderful adventures. A gentleman relates the history of his life, filling a full chapter. Another chapter stages a dialogue between Adams and his host that nearly ends badly. The return of the lovers prevents the catastrophe. Fielding mixes road adventure, talk, and moral comedy around his simple, good-hearted parson.
joshua-volume-2:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter nine, inside Pharaoh's palace. A chamberlain ushers Hosea, the Hebrew warrior, into the audience chamber. The palace lies hushed in deep mourning, its gay crowds fled from pestilence. Priests glide through infected rooms swinging silver censers of resin and juniper.

Bai, second prophet of Amon, greets Hosea cheerfully amid the drooping heads. He assures the warrior that no one blames him for his people's misdeeds. But Hosea confesses he came to beg release from military service. The priest interrupts to remind him of a debt. This volume sets Hosea's divided duty, to Pharaoh and to his own people, at its center.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-2:
Journeys Through Bookland, volume two, is Charles H. Sylvester's plan of reading in the world's best literature for children. The new edition of 1922 gathers tales, fables, and poems from many lands. Aesop opens the volume, followed by tales from the Arabian Nights. The Falcon and the Partridge and The Sparrow and the Eagle appear there.

Blake's Infant Joy and a poem by George MacDonald stand among the stories. Readers also meet Grimm's Discreet Hans, Rumpelstiltzkin, and the tale of Bluebeard. Japanese stories, including The Discontented Stonecutter and The Mirror of Matsuyama, widen the range. Sylvester aimed to lead children, step by step, into great books. This volume mixes fairy tale, fable, and verse for young readers at home.
keeping-watch-night-watches-part-2:
Keeping Watch is a set of stories by W. W. Jacobs, the second part of his Night Watches. The night-watchman narrator opens by reading character in a couple resting in their skiff below his wharf. He tells them he is a student of human nature. Then he begins the title tale, about a girl kept aboard the schooner Belle.

Her father, Captain Butt, a widower, watched over the girl too closely for her happiness. Jacobs's watchman tells such tales to pass his slow nights. Each story turns on small deceptions, courtship, and village cunning. The cozy frame, a yarn begun at the wharf, is classic Jacobs. His humor stays gentle even when his characters scheme.
king-henry-iv-part-2:
William Shakespeare wrote King Henry IV, Part 2 as the second part of Henry the Fourth. Its title page adds two key facts about its scope. It contains the death of the king, it says. It also contains the coronation of King Henry the Fifth.

Part 2 opens with an Induction spoken by Rumour alone. Rumour begs the crowd to open their ears to loud speech. Rumour says the wind serves as a post-horse from east to west. False reports and slanders ride on Rumour's tongue in every language. Rumour claims to speak of peace while hidden enmity wounds the world. That warning frames a play built from talk, report, and distrust.
king-henry-vi-part-2:
Duke Gloucester fights fierce charges at court in the passage sampled from Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 2. Gloucester says Beauford's red eyes reveal the malice in his heart. Suffolk's cloudy brow shows stormy hate, he claims. Buckingham, too, unburdens an envious load through his tongue, Gloucester adds.

Gloucester accuses York, the Queen, and others of plotting against his guiltless life. False witness and more treason charges will condemn him, he warns. The Cardinal calls his railing intolerable and orders him taken away. Gloucester warns that Henry casts away his crutch too soon. He says the shepherd is beaten from the king's side here.
kitto-cyclopaedia-1845-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Kitto's Cyclopaedia of Biblical Literature appeared in 1845 and completed the work. Kitto had planned the dictionary as the labor of his life, and deafness and poverty had not stopped him. The closing volume brought the Bible's world, from first article to last, into one finished design.

The entries run through the second half of the alphabet, covering places, rites, natural history, and the daily life behind the text. Kitto's rule holds throughout: explain Scripture by the real customs of the East, not by guesswork. Contributors added the results of new travel and excavation as the volumes grew. The great scholar's life work stands finished here, a monument of Victorian learning. For half a century, few ministers in the English-speaking world prepared a sermon far from Kitto's side.
kropotkin-memoirs-revolutionist-1899-vol:
Volume two of Kropotkin's Memoirs of a Revolutionist, also from 1899, completes his autobiography. The first volume carried him from princely childhood to Siberian service. This volume follows the exile years in Western Europe. Kropotkin joins the anarchist movement and becomes one of its leading writers.

He recalls comrades, congresses, trials, and the slow building of a movement. His science continues beside the politics, in geography and biology. The two volumes together finish the life story he chose to tell. Memoirs by revolutionaries rarely match its grace and candor. It remains the standard life of Kropotkin in his own words. Readers close it knowing the man.
l-abbe-constantin-volume-2:
Volume Two continues Ludovic Halévy's French novel The Abbé Constantin, in English. Project Gutenberg issued it as number forty-two in its French Immortals series. The series honored works crowned by the French Academy.

The story centers on a gentle village priest, the Abbé Constantin. New money and new people press against his quiet world of old faith. Kindness, rather than force, shapes how hearts change around him. Readers who finished the first volume will find the tale's warmth deepening here. The volume stands as the middle part of the complete English issue. Its priest remains the calm center while fortunes shift around him.
layamon-brut-madden-vol-2:
Volume two of Layamon's Brut, in Frederic Madden's 1847 edition with his literal English translation, continues the verse chronicle of Britain's kings. Layamon wrote around 1200, in early Middle English alliterative verse. The story now enters its richest ground: the age of Arthur.

Arthur's birth, his wars against the Saxons, his Roman campaign, and the treason of Mordred fill these pages. Layamon expands his sources with dreams, elves at Arthur's birth, and the king borne away to Avalon. His Arthur is grander and stranger than in any earlier English telling. The volume is the heart of the Brut and of early Arthurian literature.
le-morte-d-arthur-volume-2:
Volume Two of Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur continues the Round Table epic. Its contents open with Book Ten and Sir Tristram. Tristram jousts and strikes down King Arthur himself in one chapter.

Tristram also saves his rival Palomides in another chapter. The two promise to fight together within a fortnight. Sagramore and other knights cross Tristram's path in turn. Love, loyalty, and rivalry tangle as the volume proceeds. Readers reach the richer, sadder half of Arthur's world here. Tristram's love for Isolde shadows his many victories. The volume's tournaments grow darker as old loyalties strain.
lecky-england-18th-vol-2:
Walpole's long peace shapes the second volume of Lecky's History of England in the Eighteenth Century, in the 1892 printing. Jacobite risings flare and fail in Scotland and the north. Meanwhile Britain's trade and empire grow year by steady year under a calm, corrupt, stable order.

Lecky weaves politics, society, and ideas into one broad narrative. He shows how a nation grows rich while its public life sinks into jobbery. Ministers, merchants, and mobs each get their measured share of blame and praise. The volume keeps his panoramic method at full stretch, humane in judgment and vast in learning throughout.
legends-and-lyrics-part-2:
The Second Series of Adelaide Anne Procter's Legends and Lyrics continues her popular verse. This text also comes from the 1890 George Bell edition. A Legend of Provence opens the contents list.

Poems include A Lost Chord, her most famous piece of all. Others treat envy, warnings, golden days, and dreams of life. A New Mother and The Tyrant and the Captive show her range. Procter's simple music carries deep feeling about death and hope. Victorian readers kept her books beside their family Bibles. A Lost Chord alone kept her name alive for decades. Its organ music and lost faith still move modern readers.
lesage-gil-blas-smollett-1749-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Smollett's Gil Blas appeared in 1749, continuing Lesage's picaresque novel in Tobias Smollett's English. Gil Blas, the servant hero, has learned the ways of inns, stages, and sickrooms. In this volume his fortunes rise and fall in new households.

Service with quack doctors, proud nobles, and churchmen gives Gil fresh lessons in human folly. He gains money and polish, then loses ground through trust and vanity, as the form demands. Lesage used the rogue's path to satirize every rank of society. Smollett's lively translation kept the French tale an English favorite, and Volume 2 deepens both the comedy and the bite.
li-chi-legge-1885-vol-2:
Volume two of Legge's Li Chi, published in 1885 as Sacred Books of the East twenty-eight, completes the Book of Rites. The second half of the classic turns to education, music's moral power, and the conduct of rulers in detail. The famous chapter on the Great Learning's roots sits within this classic's wider family of texts.

Legge sustains his method: close translation, full notes, and respect for the commentators. Readers meet a civilization that treated manners as a branch of government. Weddings, funerals, audiences, and archery all carry rules meant to school the heart. Together the two volumes give English its complete Li Chi. Legge's Confucian translations, taken as a whole, were a life's work of rare scale.
li-ki-legge-vol-2:
Legge's second Li Ki volume completed the Book of Rites in 1885. It formed volume twenty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. The remaining ritual classics of ancient China fill its pages.

Two short treatises in this volume became famous far beyond the whole. The Great Learning teaches self-cultivation as the root of good government. The Doctrine of the Mean praises harmony, sincerity, and the balanced life. Later Chinese education made both texts central for students. Together the volumes state ancient China's vision of social order. That order runs from the family altar to the throne itself.
life-and-letters-of-charles-darwin-volum:
Volume Two of Darwin's life and letters opens in October 1859. Its first chapters cover the publication of the Origin of Species. Letters then trace how evolution spread through 1861 and 1862. Later chapters follow the Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication.

Work on man leads to the Descent of Man in 1871. Botanical letters cover flower fertilisation across forty years. Earthworms, coral reefs, and a life of Erasmus Darwin fill later pages. The volume ends with miscellaneous letters running to 1882. Second editions of Coral Reefs and the Descent also appear here. Cross and self fertilisation experiments occupy the final botanical chapter.
life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-huxley-:
Volume Two of Huxley's life and letters runs year by year. Its chapters march from 1870 through 1884 in sequence. Leonard Huxley arranged his father's correspondence within that frame. A signed 1857 photograph of the young scientist serves as frontispiece.

These were Huxley's years of public eminence in science and education. The annual chapters let readers watch controversies rise and settle. Letters show the working scientist behind the famous public voice. Paired with its companions, the volume completes a full Victorian life. A Walker and Cockerill photograph of 1857 supplies the frontispiece portrait. Chapters for 1875 and 1876 split across two entries each.
life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-the-qu:
Volume Two of Tytler's Queen Victoria life continues the reign. Royal progresses to Burghley, Stowe, and Strathfieldsaye open the contents. A powder ball and the Queen's first visit to Germany follow. Railway speculation and the failing potato crop mark the 1840s.

Princess Helena's birth and Ibrahim Pasha's visit enter the record. Prince Albert's installation as Cambridge chancellor receives a chapter. The Queen's western Scottish isles tour closes this portion. Tytler keeps close to court movements and public events throughout. Autumn yachting excursions and the Spanish marriages fill chapter five. The western islands stay at Ardverikie closes the listed contents.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-2:
Part Two begins with Chapter 6, a cub-pilot's experience. The Paul Jones took two weeks from Cincinnati to New Orleans. Rocks at Louisville and other delays slowed the voyage. A pilot befriended young Twain and taught him to steer.

A deck passenger borrowed six dollars and never repaid them. Twain jokes the youth probably died, since he never returned. His Amazon exploration scheme collapses for lack of money and ships. So he plans a siege against his pilot for a new career. Deck passage meant steerage, Twain explains in a footnote. The Paul Jones now bound for St. Louis offered his next chance.
